title.en: Electricity: magnetic and heating effects of current

text.en: Mohini and Aakarsh see a working model of a lifting electromagnet. It lifts iron nails when the current is on and drops them when it is off.

An electric current in a wire produces a magnetic field around it, which we can detect with a compass needle.
Hans Christian Oersted discovered this when a compass needle deflected near a wire carrying current.
A coil of insulated wire wound on an iron nail and connected to a cell becomes an electromagnet that picks up iron paper clips.
The magnetism lasts only while current flows, so an electromagnet is temporary and can be switched on and off.
Its strength can be increased by adding more turns of wire or by using a stronger current.
Electromagnets are used in electric bells, cranes, motors, fans and loudspeakers.
Electric current also produces heat when it flows through a wire, called the heating effect of current.
Wires that resist current more, like the thin nichrome wire in heaters, get hot enough to glow.
Heating effect is used in heaters, irons, toasters and bulbs, and in fuses, which melt and break the circuit if the current is too high.
An MCB switches off the circuit automatically in case of overload, and we should never touch bare wires with wet hands.

problem.en: How can you make an electromagnet stronger?

text.en: Wind more turns of wire around the iron core.

why.en: More turns increase the magnetic field.

text.en: Use a stronger cell or more cells.
Test by counting how many paper clips it lifts.

prompt.en: Why is an electromagnet useful in a crane?

requiredIdeas.en: It can be switched on to lift iron.
It can be switched off to drop it.

points.en: Current has a magnetic effect, so a coil makes an electromagnet.
